content: The nasal helm is a type of helmet that gained popularity during the late Dark Ages and continued to be widely used throughout the Early Medieval period. This helmet design featured a domed or raised center, typically constructed around a basic skull-cap structure. A distinctive characteristic of the nasal helm was a single protruding strip, or nasal guard, that extended downward over the nose, providing additional protection to the face. The nasal helm began to appear across Europe in the late 9th century and quickly became the dominant form of head protection. It replaced earlier designs such as the pudding-bowl helmet and the spectacle helm. One of the earliest known examples of this type of helmet is the Vasgaard Helm. The Bayeux Tapestry, a famous historical artifact, depicts numerous examples of nasal helms, highlighting their widespread use and popularity during that era. By the 13th century, the nasal helm gradually fell out of favor as helmets offering more comprehensive facial protection were developed. Despite losing popularity among the higher classes of knights and men-at-arms, nasal helms continued to be used by archers, for whom an unobstructed field of vision was essential. Nasal helms have been discovered in both one-piece and spangenhelm constructions. Helmets from the later period of their use were often crafted as a single, smooth, raised dome. This design allowed weapons to glance off the surface more easily, enhancing the wearer’s protection.
